documents.title: Guidelines for the Use of Generative AI Tools
documents.summary: A 2023 letter from the provost and two vice presidents encourages the community to experiment with AI and sets six general guidelines on confidential data, public-by-default input, academic integrity, bias and verification, credentials and procurement. Course-level permission is left to instructors, whom it asks to give clear instructions and attribution rules.
documents.stance_why: The letter says "We encourage you to experiment with AI tools" but sets no rule for coursework itself: "Faculty members are expected to provide clear instructions on the permitted use of generative AI tools" and students "are expected to follow their instructors' guidelines." The decision is handed to instructors, so delegates.

units.why: The letter says "We encourage you to experiment with AI tools," an explicit welcome of AI use addressed to the whole community, so it is a default-permissive stance (P02), encourage, general phase.
units.anchor: We encourage you to experiment with AI tools.

units.why: "this technology will transform how we learn, teach, conduct research, and carry out daily tasks" is an impact claim with no rule, so informs. P87 (benefits) is the nearest type but the sentence says "transform," not a named benefit.
units.anchor: this technology will transform how we learn, teach, conduct research
units.frag_start: While its precise impacts are unknown
units.fit_note: States that AI will transform learning, teaching, research and daily tasks and that impacts are unknown; a general impact claim rather than a named benefit.

units.why: The guidelines "align with existing university policies and uphold our institutional commitment to safety, security, and academic integrity," so AI use must follow existing policy: P77. P56 (framework) fits less well because the sentence stresses alignment, not new principles.
units.anchor: which align with existing university policies

units.why: "Do not enter confidential or legally restricted data ... into an AI tool" forbids inputting restricted data, addressed to everyone, about privacy: P50 with must-not.
units.anchor: Do not enter confidential or legally restricted data
units.frag_end: moderate or high-risk into an AI tool.

units.why: "Treat all information shared with an AI tool as if it will become public" and the warning that input "may be retained" tell users to assume prompts are stored, a privacy rule: P50.
units.anchor: Treat all information shared with an AI tool as if it will become public.
units.policy: Treat all information shared with an AI tool as if it will become public; do not share personal or sensitive information, because input may be retained.

units.why: "All students and faculty are expected to know and adhere to their school's academic integrity policies" ties AI use to existing integrity rules, so P77 (comply with existing policy) with must for all.
units.anchor: expected to know and adhere to their school's academic integrity policies
units.frag_start: All students and faculty are expected

units.why: "Faculty members are expected to provide clear instructions on the permitted use of generative AI tools for academic work and requirements for attribution" obliges instructors to state AI rules in course materials: P09.
units.anchor: Faculty members are expected to provide clear instructions on the permitted use

units.why: "students are expected to follow their instructors' guidelines about permitted use of AI for coursework" makes students responsible for following each instructor's rule: P78. P04 is not chosen because the actor is the student and the duty is to follow.
units.anchor: students are expected to follow their instructors' guidelines about permitted use of AI
units.fit_note: Also implies that instructors, not the university, decide permitted use (P04).

units.why: "AI-generated responses can be biased, inaccurate, inappropriate, or may contain unauthorized copyrighted information" warns that output can be wrong or biased: P31.
units.anchor: AI-generated responses can be biased, inaccurate, inappropriate

units.why: "We are each responsible for the content of our work product" states ownership of what one produces, so P29.
units.anchor: We are each responsible for the content of our work product.

units.why: "Always review and verify outputs generated by AI tools, especially before publication" is a directive to check AI output: P31.
units.anchor: Always review and verify outputs generated by AI tools

units.why: "Never share your Yale NetID and password with AI tools" is an account-credential rule about security, so P126 is closer than P50 (personal data).
units.anchor: Never share your Yale NetID and password with AI tools

units.why: "always be aware of phishing schemes" with the pointer to cybersafe practices is security awareness, P75.
units.anchor: always be aware of phishing schemes

units.why: "please conduct an initial review of the tool to ensure that it conforms to institutional security requirements" asks anyone acquiring an AI product to review it first and use the purchasing portal: tool review before purchase, P65.
units.anchor: conduct an initial review of the tool to ensure that it conforms to institutional

units.why: "The university is working to support procurement practices that coordinate shared interests and minimize institutional risk" describes the institution coordinating AI procurement, an administrative review practice: P65.
units.anchor: support procurement practices that coordinate shared interests and minimize institutional risk
units.frag_start: The university is working to support

units.why: "For up-to-date recommendations on teaching and learning, please visit the Poorvu Center's webpage" and the staff-guidelines pointer send readers to further guidance: P115.
units.anchor: For up-to-date recommendations on teaching and learning, please visit

units.why: "Generative AI is evolving quickly, as is institutional support for utilizing these tools" acknowledges that guidance changes, so P54.
units.anchor: Generative AI is evolving quickly, as is institutional support
units.fit_note: Says guidance changes with the technology but states no review schedule.

units.why: "we will embrace technological tools and harness their power for innovation. We must do this safely and responsibly" is the institution's overall commitment, a framework principle: P56 with encourage.
units.anchor: we will embrace technological tools and harness their power for innovation.

documents.unit: Poorvu Center for Teaching and Learning
documents.title: Guiding Principles: Teaching and Learning with AI
documents.summary: The Poorvu Center sets out principles on ownership and learning, reflective discussion with students, attention to how AI is changing disciplines, and ethical use (privacy, student responsibility, transparency, broader impacts). It gives instructors full authority over AI use in their courses and names no default rule.
documents.stance_why: The text says "instructors at Yale have full authority to determine whether and how students may use AI when completing assignments" and that some courses "restrict" while others "incorporate AI practices more fully." It sets no university rule and names no default, so delegates.

units.why: "if students rely on AI assistance before building their own skills, the result can be a loss of the struggle that deepens learning" gives skill-building as the reason to limit AI: P41.
units.anchor: if students rely on AI assistance before building their own skills
units.frag_start: But if students rely on AI

units.why: "AI tools can assist with familiar tasks, allowing experienced thinkers to work more effectively" names a benefit of AI without a rule: P87.
units.anchor: AI tools can assist with familiar tasks, allowing experienced thinkers to work more effectively
units.frag_start: At the same time, AI tools can assist

units.why: "Much of the Poorvu Center's guidance focuses on scaffolding assignments to preserve learning spaces" describes assignment redesign as the center's approach: P35, though it reports a focus and not a rule.
units.anchor: scaffolding assignments to preserve learning spaces
units.fit_note: Describes the center's guidance focus on scaffolding rather than a rule on a specific redesign.

units.why: "Generative AI tools should be used in ways that allow students and faculty to take deeper ownership of their work" is a principle that AI use should support ownership; P29 is nearest since it covers ownership of work.
units.anchor: should be used in ways that allow students and faculty to take deeper ownership
units.frag_start: Generative AI tools should be used
units.fit_note: Frames ownership as a design principle for AI use, not only responsibility for submitted work.

units.why: "Are you the author or maker of the work? ... If it's writing, is it in your voice?" are questions to ask before using AI, expressing that the student stays the primary author: P32.
units.anchor: Are you the author or maker of the work?
units.frag_start: Decisions around using AI should consider

units.why: "faculty should reflect on whether students' use of AI supports genuine learning" tells instructors to base course AI decisions on learning aims: P83.
units.anchor: faculty should reflect on whether students' use of AI supports genuine learning
units.frag_start: When designing their courses, faculty should

units.why: "instructors at Yale have full authority to determine whether and how students may use AI when completing assignments" gives the decision to each instructor: P04.
units.anchor: instructors at Yale have full authority to determine whether and how students may use AI
units.frag_start: Within each course, instructors at Yale

units.why: "developed as part of a deep and ongoing conversation" asks that AI guidelines come out of discussion with disciplinary expertise about how learning is affected: P66 is the nearest type (discuss rules) but the conversation here is about designing the rule.
units.anchor: developed as part of a deep and ongoing conversation
units.fit_note: The conversation is about designing the guideline with disciplinary expertise, not only explaining it to students.

units.why: "the conversation must welcome students' voices explaining how and why they might choose to use AI" requires student participation in setting AI expectations: P67.
units.anchor: the conversation must welcome students' voices

units.why: "Creating a shared understanding around the costs and benefits of different uses of AI will benefit both students and instructors" explains why shared understanding is worth building: P66.
units.anchor: Creating a shared understanding around the costs and benefits of different uses of AI

units.why: "Instructors are encouraged to discuss with students how AI is influencing their discipline and its methods" recommends discussing AI in class: P66.
units.anchor: Instructors are encouraged to discuss with students how AI is influencing their discipline

units.why: "In some courses, it will make sense to restrict use of AI while students develop skills and become oriented to a field" accepts restriction early while skills develop: P08.
units.anchor: it will make sense to restrict use of AI while students develop skills
units.frag_start: In some courses, it will make sense
units.fit_note: Says restriction suits the skill-building period but does not say when it lifts.

units.why: "Some courses may choose to incorporate AI practices more fully so that students can better understand how using AI shifts habits" permits building AI into a course: P79.
units.anchor: Some courses may choose to incorporate AI practices more fully

units.why: "Settings for these limits need to be discussed transparently as part of bringing students into the field" requires instructors to state limits openly: P66.
units.anchor: Settings for these limits need to be discussed transparently

units.why: "Instructors must safeguard student data, intellectual property, and autonomy when integrating AI tools into coursework" is a binding duty on instructors about privacy and IP: P50.
units.anchor: Instructors must safeguard student data, intellectual property, and autonomy

units.why: "Yale-approved platforms should be used when AI is required, because they ensure greater privacy protections" prefers vetted tools when AI is required: P92 (approved tools). P79 not chosen because it does not itself require AI.
units.anchor: Yale-approved platforms should be used when AI is required
units.fit_note: Applies when an instructor requires AI use, and gives privacy as the reason.

units.why: "Students are responsible for using AI in ways that uphold the ethical standards of their courses and disciplines" makes students answerable for how they use AI: P29.
units.anchor: Students are responsible for using AI in ways that uphold the ethical standards
units.frag_start: Students are responsible for using AI

units.why: "detailed in the course syllabus or in the instructions for each course assignment" says where instructor-set standards are written. P09 (rules stated in syllabus or assignment) fits; P78 not chosen because it is a duty on students to look it up.
units.anchor: detailed in the course syllabus or in the instructions for each course assignment
units.frag_start: These standards are set by instructors

units.why: "Faculty and students should cite their use of AI" is a disclosure expectation for everyone: P24.
units.anchor: Faculty and students should cite their use of AI.

units.why: "When instructors thoughtfully acknowledge how AI has supported their work ... they help students develop a more mature understanding" asks instructors to disclose their own AI use: P47.
units.anchor: instructors thoughtfully acknowledge how AI has supported their work
units.fit_note: Also frames the disclosure as modelling for students (P112).

units.why: "AI tools emerge from systems that affect labor, sustainability, and equity" names ethical and environmental harms: P53.
units.anchor: AI tools emerge from systems that affect labor, sustainability, and equity.

units.why: "Instructors are encouraged to acknowledge these broader implications openly with students" recommends discussing AI's harms with students. P53 chosen for the content (harms and ethical commitments); P66 fits less well because the point is the harms.
units.anchor: Instructors are encouraged to acknowledge these broader implications openly with students
units.fit_note: Also an instruction to discuss the harms with students (P66).

documents.title: AI Guidelines (student guidance page)
documents.summary: A landing page quoting the Yale Task Force on AI and describing the center's AI guidance for students and teachers. It welcomes AI use for learning, tells students to follow individual course policies, and links to principles, an AI literacy framework and the Clarity AI platform.
documents.stance_why: The page says AI "may be used to enhance student learning in a variety of ways" but asks students to use tools "in compliance with individual course policies and guidelines." It sets no rule of its own and sends decisions to courses, so delegates.

units.why: The Task Force quote, "we encourage our colleagues across Yale to proactively lead the development of AI by utilizing, critiquing, and examining the technology," welcomes AI use and critical engagement: P02.
units.anchor: we encourage our colleagues across Yale to proactively lead the development of AI
units.frag_start: Rather than wait to see how AI will develop

units.why: "These principles are intended to support conversations and reflective decision-making about generative AI" states the purpose of the principles: P56.
units.anchor: These principles are intended to support conversations and reflective decision-making

units.why: "students must be prepared to lead in an AI-infused world" gives preparation for AI-rich work as a reason to engage with AI: P44.
units.anchor: students must be prepared to lead in an AI-infused world
units.frag_start: we understand that students must be prepared

units.why: "Generative AI may be used to enhance student learning in a variety of ways, ranging from summarization to problem-solving" permits and welcomes a range of uses, a default-permissive position: P02.
units.anchor: Generative AI may be used to enhance student learning in a variety of ways

units.why: "in compliance with individual course policies and guidelines" says students use AI under each course's rules: P78.
units.anchor: in compliance with individual course policies and guidelines
units.frag_start: The Poorvu Center works with students to prioritize

units.why: "We work with faculty to help evolve curricula to incorporate discussions around AI into course content" describes the center supporting faculty: P63.
units.anchor: We work with faculty to help evolve curricula to incorporate discussions around AI
units.frag_start: We work with faculty to help evolve

units.why: "provide resources and guidance to assist in making informed decisions about whether or not to infuse AI in their teaching" shows the center supports an instructor-level choice: P63.
units.anchor: provide resources and guidance to assist in making informed decisions

units.why: "The University is committed to investing in AI technology and resources to assist students, faculty, and staff" is an institutional capacity commitment: P122.
units.anchor: committed to investing in AI technology and resources
units.frag_start: The University is committed to investing

units.why: "Only then can we make educated and informed decisions about whether or not to incorporate its use in the classroom" frames the decision to use AI as one made after weighing benefits and limits: P118.
units.anchor: make educated and informed decisions about whether or not to incorporate its use
units.fit_note: Institutional framing of why the university studies AI; not directed at one user decision.

units.why: "Yale has the opportunity to serve as a model by adapting its curricula to prepare students to lead" is an aspiration to prepare students for AI-rich work: P44.
units.anchor: adapting its curricula to prepare students to lead in advancing and considering

documents.title: Academic Dishonesty (Undergraduate Regulations)
documents.summary: The Yale College integrity regulations contain one paragraph on AI: unattributed AI-generated text violates academic integrity, and unauthorized AI use may too. Whether AI is allowed is left to each instructor, and students must check first. The rest of the document covers cheating, plagiarism and collaboration generally.
documents.stance_why: The AI note says "How and whether instructors permit you to use AI writing tools at Yale will vary widely from course to course, and is always subject to each instructor's authority and policy." Unauthorized use is a breach, but what is authorized is left to instructors, so delegates.

units.why: "Inserting AI-generated text into an assignment without proper attribution is a violation of academic integrity" classes unattributed AI text as misconduct: P36. P24 (disclosure) fits too, but the sentence names the violation.
units.anchor: Inserting AI-generated text into an assignment without proper attribution is a violation of academic integrity
units.fit_note: Also requires attribution of AI-generated text (P24).

units.why: "using AI tools in a manner that was not authorized by your instructor may also be considered a breach of academic integrity" makes unauthorized use misconduct: P36.
units.anchor: using AI tools in a manner that was not authorized by your instructor
units.frag_start: and using AI tools in a manner
units.fit_note: Implies AI use not authorized by the instructor is off limits, a fallback rule (P06).

units.why: "How and whether instructors permit you to use AI writing tools at Yale will vary widely from course to course, and is always subject to each instructor's authority" delegates to instructors: P04.
units.anchor: How and whether instructors permit you to use AI writing tools at Yale

units.why: "Always check with your instructor before using these tools to produce your Yale coursework" tells students to ask before using AI: P10.
units.anchor: Always check with your instructor before using these tools

units.why: "Guidelines about these practices may change over time, so be sure to ask for the most up to date policy" says the policy is provisional: P54.
units.anchor: Guidelines about these practices may change over time
units.frag_start: Guidelines about these practices may change
units.fit_note: Also tells students to ask for the current policy (P10).

units.why: "For a fuller discussion of these issues, see the Poorvu Center for Teaching and Learning pages on AI Guidelines" points to further guidance: P115.
units.anchor: see the Poorvu Center for Teaching and Learning pages on AI Guidelines
units.frag_start: For a fuller discussion of these issues

units.why: "the standard penalty is two semesters of suspension" for cheating states a concrete penalty; it names cheating, not AI, and applies to AI misuse only through the AI note that calls it a breach of integrity: P37.
units.anchor: the standard penalty is two semesters of suspension
units.frag_start: Yale regards cheating as a serious
units.fit_note: About cheating generally; does not name AI.

units.why: "they are not demonstrating what they have learned, but are rather doing the very work of synthesis" explains that writing yourself is the learning, a skill-building rationale although AI is not named: P41.
units.anchor: doing the very work of synthesis
units.fit_note: Does not mention AI; it explains why students producing their own writing matters.

units.why: "students who turn in someone else's work, therefore, are giving away the very substance of their educations" grounds integrity in lost learning: P41.
units.anchor: students who turn in someone else's work, therefore, are giving away the very substance
units.frag_start: Writing is one of the most powerful sites of learning

notes: Only the four included university-layer documents were coded. Poorvu AI Guidance for Students/Instructors subpages were not fetched. The academic-dishonesty regulation is general and AI appears in one paragraph; two rationale units from its general integrity preface are coded P41 although they do not name AI.
